newsitem.title: FRANCE: Details of French audit and tax measures.
newsitem.headline: Details of French audit and tax measures.

text.p: An audit of public finances ordered by France's new Socialist-led government showed the public deficit running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent of gross domestic product. The government said it planned to reduce this by around 0.4 percentage points to help qualify for European monetary union. Following are details:
AUDIT
The audit was carried out by two members of the Court of Auditors, Philippe Nasse and Jacques Bonnet.
It forecast the 1997 total public deficit, which comprises central government spending, welfare and local authority spending, at between 3.5 and 3.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
The 1997 Finance Act voted under the previous conservative government predicted a deficit of 3.0 percent of GDP.
The deficit widened by 27 to 37 billion francs due to a 15 to 17 billion franc tax revenue shortfall and a 12 to 20 billion franc spending overshoot, the audit found.

The auditors found that the central government budget deficit would be between 312 to 322 billion francs with the welfare shortfall between 44 billion and 49 billion francs. The social security deficit figure includes a 35 billion to 38 billion franc gap in the central social security account.
The 1997 Finance Act had forecast the government deficit would be 285 billion francs and the central social security gap 30 billion francs.
The audit saw the surplus in local authority and other state agency funds at between 26.5 and 28.5 billion francs.
The report noted a previously expected 12 billion franc surplus in national unemployment fund UNEDIC has been spent.

The auditors said their estimates were based on forecasts made by national statistics institute INSEE in June, which saw growth rising 2.3 percent this year. They also warned the government the estimate was based on incomplete data for 1997.
1997 BUDGET REDUCTION MEASURES

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said the government planned deficit-reduction measures worth 32 billion francs, equivalent to 0.4 percentage points of GDP. But he said the government was not setting a precise target for this year.
Revenue is to be raised by 22 billion francs and spending cut by 10 billion francs. There were no measures affecting households. Strauss-Kahn announced the following:

-- A rise in company taxes. The government left the basic rate of tax on corporate profits unchanged at 33.3 percent but added a 15 percent surcharge for 1997 and 1998. This is on top of a 10 percent surcharge introduced in 1995. The measure brings the effective tax rate to 41.6 percent from 36.6 currently.
-- Capital gains tax to be raised to 41.6 percent from 19 percent and from now on will be treated the same as corporate tax on profits.
-- Tax on share sales remains unchanged at the lower rate.
-- Businesses with revenues of less than 50 million francs a year exempted from the measures.

-- The tax rise applies for 1997 and 1998 and will be cut progressively from then on. In 1999 the new surcharge will be cut to 10 percent from 15 percent and the effective tax rate will be 39.9 percent. The government gave no details for plans to reduce the surcharge beyond 1999.
-- Capital gains tax rise will raise six billion francs and company tax rise will raise 16 billion francs.
-- State-owned companies may make budget contributions. The government traditionally taps state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC) for funds to fill budget gaps.
-- Two billion francs of 10 billion in spending cuts to come from defence budget
1997 BUDGET ACCORDING TO PREVIOUS GOVERNMENT
A leaked letter from former prime minister Alain Juppe to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, dated June 2, gave the following details on the 1997 budget:

-- Total revenues were seen around 35 billion francs less than expected, due to a 15 billion franc shortfall in central government revenues, mainly VAT (sales tax), a 10 billion franc shortfall in payroll taxes to finance welfare spending and the loss from the budget of a nearly 12 billion franc surplus previously expected from national unemployment fund UNEDIC.

-- Total spending needs were seen at 23 billion francs more than expected, partially offset by five billion franc savings on debt service charges and a centre-right spending freeze on 10 billion francs in credit lines. Juppe said this would leave only eight billion francs to be covered.
The new government however has since partially reversed the 10 billion franc spending freeze.
The audit took account of some 11 billion francs in new spending measures already announced by the new government, but offset this against the 10 billion francs spending freeze.
1997 WELFARE DEFICIT

The central social security accounts, which use payroll taxes to fund pensions, healthcare and family benefits, are expected to show a deficit of 35 to 38 billion francs, compared to 30 billion francs originally expected, the audit found.
Including other welfare accounts, the total welfare deficit could be 44 to 49 billion francs, the audit said.
The government could save some money on welfare this year through a plan to limit family allowances for the higher paid.
ACCUMULATED WELFARE DEFICIT

Juppe warned the government it needed to take action this summer to deal with the accumulated welfare deficit in 1996 and 1997 to prevent cash-flow problems. The welfare system is currently being financed by temporary advances from state bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations.

Strauss-Kahn said the government would study how to deal with the accumulated deficit, as well as any reforms of payroll taxes, in the autumn, at the same time as its holds a national conference on jobs and considers a law on welfare funding.
1998 BUDGET
Strauss-Kahn said the 1998 budget bill would aim to reduce the public deficit to three percent of GDP.

Juppe in his letter warned that the trend in public deficits pointed to a figure above four percent of GDP next year but said this could be cut to three percent "after savings on budget and welfare spending, questioning some fiscal spending and tapping exceptional non-fiscal revenues."
Economic growth was not having a strong enough effect on government and welfare revenues to allow the deficit to fall spontaneously, Juppe said.
